input:
This pricing case examines the break-even position of a SaaS tier. The tier is priced at $374 per unit, with a variable cost of $187 per unit and fixed costs of $282k per year. On this basis, the break-even volume works out to 1508 units per year. Current volume, however, is 801 units per year, which means that the tier is currently selling well below the volume it needs in order to break even. Each unit sold contributes the difference between the price and the variable cost toward covering the fixed costs, and at 801 units that contribution covers only part of the $282k, leaving the tier short of break-even by the contribution on the missing volume.

It is worth noting that the volume figures used here are last year's actuals, so the comparison effectively describes where the tier stood over the course of that year at the stated price and costs. One important quantity is, however, missing from the case: the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated. As a result, the break-even figure answers a fixed-price question, namely what volume the present price and cost structure requires, and it does not show what a different price would do, because the volume response that a price change would produce is precisely the quantity that has not been estimated.

The tier is priced at $374 per unit with a variable cost of $187 per unit and fixed costs of $282k per year, which puts break-even at 1508 units per year; current volume is 801 units per year. The gap between the two volumes is the finding: each unit sold contributes the difference between price and variable cost toward the fixed costs, and at 801 units that contribution covers only part of the $282k, leaving the tier short of break-even by the contribution on the missing volume.

The volume figures are last year's actuals, so the comparison states where the tier stood over that year at the stated price and costs. Neither figure is a forecast: the break-even volume and the current volume are both built from last year's volumes and the present price and cost values, and they move when any of those inputs moves. One quantity is missing from the case. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated, and the break-even figure therefore answers a fixed-price question: what volume the present price and cost structure requires. It does not show what a different price would do, because the volume response that a price change would produce is the very quantity that has not been estimated.
